conventional morality|conventional level: Kohlberg's stages 3 and 4, "conventional role conformity" (slide 16), where people have been "socialized into accepting the customary moral attitudes and judgements" of family, community, the corporate world and society (course notes); a poor guide to the extent those attitudes are "flawed or may be only accidentally right". See [Convention can be flawed or only accidentally right, so the levels go past it](#/libs7102-l2/why-conventional-is-not-final).
conflict of interest: A choice between being "loyal to the company" and serving "your own interest" (slide 3), such as "offering paid services on the side to a client of your company". See [Conventional morality is doing what your co-workers and your boss would do](#/libs7102-l2/conflicts-of-interest-and-convention).
Kohlberg's stages|stages of moral develo: "6 stages of moral development – how morality is perceived at each stage (grouped in 3 main levels)": preconventional 1 obedience and punishment, 2 individualism and exchange; conventional 3 good boy/good girl, 4 law and order; 4.5 the cynic; postconventional 5 social contract and individual rights, 6 universal moral principles (slide 16). See [Kohlberg's six stages run from fear of punishment to universal principles](#/libs7102-l2/piaget-and-kohlberg-six-stages).
law and order (stage 4): Kohlberg's stage 4, "the good citizen": "concern with society as a whole"; conventional morality "adds justification - laws are useful for social order"; "Authority figures are seldom questioned. Many adults never reach the third level (stages 5 and 6)" (slide 20). See [Kohlberg's six stages run from fear of punishment to universal principles](#/libs7102-l2/piaget-and-kohlberg-six-stages).
the cynic (stage 4.5)|stage 4.5: "Conventional morality seen as socially constructed, relative and arbitrary. Conventions and tradition are questioned. But no alternative is known"; "Wise enough to question it all, not wise enough to find answers" (slide 21). See [Kohlberg's six stages run from fear of punishment to universal principles](#/libs7102-l2/piaget-and-kohlberg-six-stages).
tyranny of the majority: "Suppose that a majority decides to elect someone who hurts a minority, the so-called 'tyranny of the majority' (John Stuart Mill, Thomas Jefferson)": the realization "that even democratic processes may fail" that marks stage 6 (slide 23). See [Convention can be flawed or only accidentally right, so the levels go past it](#/libs7102-l2/why-conventional-is-not-final).
civil disobedience: Stage 6's "distinguishing issue": "If a law cannot be changed by democratic processes, disobedience can be morally justified"; Martin Luther King argued "that laws are only valid insofar as they are grounded in justice" (slide 23). See [Convention can be flawed or only accidentally right, so the levels go past it](#/libs7102-l2/why-conventional-is-not-final).
know-how (moral knowledge)|knowing-that: Stages of moral development suggest that "moral knowledge could be know-how/a skill rather than knowing-that", not "the ability of memorizing certain claims (e.g. 'lying is wrong')" (slide 14). See [Kohlberg's six stages run from fear of punishment to universal principles](#/libs7102-l2/piaget-and-kohlberg-six-stages).
equality as a moral ideal: Singer: "Equality is a moral ideal, not a statement of a fact"; "we are obviously not the same!"; the ideal is impartiality, utilitarianism's "equal consideration of interests" (slide 27). Equal rights, not the same rights: "Pigs cannot vote" (slide 26). See [Singer: equality means equal consideration of interests, and the test is suffering](#/libs7102-l2/singer-all-animals-are-equal).
Can they suffer?: Bentham's question, quoted by Singer: "The question is not: can they talk or reason, but... 'Can they suffer?'"; "the capacity for suffering as the vital characteristic that gives a being the right to equal consideration", in place of merit (slide 28). See [Singer: equality means equal consideration of interests, and the test is suffering](#/libs7102-l2/singer-all-animals-are-equal).
speciesism|speciesist: A bias towards one's own species: "The experimenter shows a bias towards his own species when he refuses to test on an infant, but will test on a guinea pig" (slide 29); "we simply prefer animals of our species. Most of us are speciesists" (slide 31). See [Singer: equality means equal consideration of interests, and the test is suffering](#/libs7102-l2/singer-all-animals-are-equal).
